question.text: A block of mass m is pressed flat against the vertical side face of a much larger block of mass M (the wedge), as the figure shows; block m has no surface beneath it and stays in place purely because of friction against the wedge's face, with a friction coefficient μ between the two surfaces. A horizontal push F drives the wedge (and the smaller block moves along with it). What is the least value F can take so that the smaller block does not slide down relative to the wedge?
conditions: wedge has mass M, block has mass m
friction coefficient between wedge and block is μ
block m has no support underneath it, held up only by friction against the wedge's vertical face
block m must stay stationary relative to the wedge, i.e. move together with it

figure.description: A large block of mass M (the wedge) stands on the ground. A horizontal force F pushes it from the left, shown by an arrow. A smaller block of mass m touches the wedge's right-hand vertical face; this smaller block has nothing beneath it and is kept from falling only by friction against the wedge's surface. As F acts, the wedge and the smaller block accelerate together horizontally.

solution.approach: The block m is held up only by friction against the wedge's vertical face, and that friction comes from the normal force created by the sideways acceleration.

steps.text: Since M and m move together, they share one horizontal acceleration.
The wedge pushes block m sideways, so the normal force N between them equals m times that acceleration.
The block has nothing below it, so friction alone must support its weight; for the minimum F, friction is at its maximum value.
Put N = ma into this and solve for a.
steps.equation: μ m a = mg ⇒ a = g/μ
steps.why_this_step: This is the smallest sideways acceleration at which the available friction is exactly enough to hold the block up.

steps.text: Put a = g/μ into the system equation and solve for F.

common_mistakes.text: Leaving block m's own mass out of the accelerating system and writing F = M g / μ instead of (M+m) g / μ.
